meta.titre: Earth-Sun Relationships: rotation, revolution and the seasons
meta.sous_theme: Rotation, revolution, tilt of the axis, solstices, equinoxes and time

sections.contenu_markdown: In Cameroon the day and the night are almost equal in length all year, but in Europe the evenings in June stay bright until late and the days in December are short. This difference comes from the way the Earth moves around the Sun. The GCE paper often asks for the season on a given date, for the position of the overhead Sun, or for the difference between rotation and revolution. A student who understands the two movements and the tilt of the axis can answer all of these without learning separate facts.

items: The Earth is a sphere and the equator is the line of 0° latitude.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23½°N and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23½°S.
Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole.

sections.titre: How the Earth's movements make day, night and seasons
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Two movements
| | Rotation | Revolution |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | The Earth spins on its axis, the line through the poles | The Earth travels round the Sun along its orbit |
| Time taken | About 24 hours | About 365¼ days |
| Direction | West to east | Anticlockwise when seen from above the North Pole |
| Main effects | Day and night, time differences, apparent deflection of winds and ocean currents | The seasons and the changing length of day and night |

### The tilted axis
The Earth's axis is tilted by 23½° from the vertical, which means that it makes an angle of 66½° with the plane of its orbit. During the whole revolution the axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space. As a result, first the Northern Hemisphere and then the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun. The hemisphere leaning towards the Sun gets more direct rays and longer days, so it has summer.

### Key dates
| Date (about) | Where the Sun is overhead at noon | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 21 March | Equator | Equinox: day and night equal everywhere. Spring begins in the north, autumn in the south |
| 21 June | Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) | Northern summer, longest day in the north. Winter in the south |
| 23 September | Equator | Equinox. Autumn in the north, spring in the south |
| 22 December | Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S) | Northern winter, shortest day in the north. Summer in the south |

The Sun can never be overhead beyond the two tropics. Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66½° N and S) there are days with 24 hours of daylight and days with 24 hours of darkness. Near the equator, day length and temperature change little through the year, and the seasons are shown by rainfall.

variantes.nom: Proofs that the Earth is spherical
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to explain proofs, evidence or reasons for the shape of the Earth
variantes.contenu_markdown: Explain each proof in a full sentence: (1) A ship moving away disappears hull first and the mast last, because the surface curves. (2) In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always curved. (3) Explorers sailed continuously in one direction and returned to their starting point. (4) Photographs taken from space show a round Earth. (5) The Pole Star appears higher in the sky as one travels north. Name the proof and then say how it shows the shape.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for the local time of a place or the longitude of a ship
variantes.contenu_markdown: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so it turns **15° in 1 hour**, which is **4 minutes for every degree**. Time difference in hours = difference in longitude $\div$ 15. Places east of a point are **ahead** of it, and places west are **behind**. Greenwich (0°) gives Greenwich Mean Time.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to explain why a season happens in one hemisphere
variantes.contenu_markdown: Build the answer in four links: the tilt of the axis, the axis keeping its direction, the position of the Earth on that date, and the consequence for sunlight and temperature. State the hemisphere each time. Never use distance from the Sun as the cause.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer when the Southern Hemisphere has winter in the month of June.

etapes.action: State the cause: the tilt of the axis.
etapes.justification: The seasons exist only because the axis is not upright. Without a tilt, every place would have the same day length all year.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The axis is tilted at 23½° from the vertical.

etapes.action: Add that the axis keeps the same direction during revolution.
etapes.justification: This explains why the hemisphere facing the Sun changes during the year.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The North end of the axis points in the same direction in space as the Earth moves round the Sun.

etapes.action: Place the Earth on its orbit on 21 June.
etapes.justification: On this date the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, and the northern part of the Earth receives more direct rays.

etapes.action: Give the consequence for both hemispheres.
etapes.justification: The examiner wants both halves of the question.
etapes.resultat_markdown: North: longer days, more heating, summer. South: leaning away, shorter days, slanting rays, winter.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer: The Earth's axis is tilted by 23½° and always points in the same direction as the Earth revolves round the Sun. In June the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, and the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. The north therefore receives more direct rays and has longer days, so it has summer. At the same time the Southern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun, receives slanting rays and has shorter days, so it has winter.

items.erreur_markdown: "We have summer because the Earth is nearer to the Sun at that time."
items.pourquoi_faux: Seasons are not caused by distance from the Sun. The cause is the tilt of the axis, which changes how directly the Sun's rays strike each hemisphere.
items.correction_markdown: In June the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun and gets more direct rays and longer days, so it has summer.

items.erreur_markdown: "Rotation is the Earth going round the Sun in 365 days."
items.pourquoi_faux: The two terms are swapped. Rotation is the spin on the axis.
items.correction_markdown: **Rotation:** spinning on the axis in about 24 hours, which causes day and night. **Revolution:** travelling round the Sun in about 365¼ days, which causes the seasons.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Sun is overhead at the equator on 21 June."
items.pourquoi_faux: On 21 June the overhead Sun has reached its northern limit.
items.correction_markdown: On 21 June the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. It is overhead at the equator on about 21 March and 23 September.

items.erreur_markdown: "On 21 March the day is long in the north and short in the south."
items.pourquoi_faux: 21 March is an equinox. The Sun is overhead at the equator, so every place has about 12 hours of day and 12 of night.
items.correction_markdown: Long days in the north and short days in the south belong to the June solstice. The reverse is true in December.

items.erreur_markdown: "A place at 45°E has a clock 3 hours behind Greenwich, because it is east of it."
items.pourquoi_faux: The Earth rotates from west to east, so places to the east see the Sun earlier and their clocks show a later time.
items.correction_markdown: 45° $\div$ 15 = 3 hours. A place at 45°E is **3 hours ahead** of Greenwich.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) On about which date is the Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn? (b) What season does the Northern Hemisphere have then?
items.solution_markdown: (a) About **22 December**. (b) **Winter**, because the Northern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun at that time.

items.enonce_markdown: It is 09:00 at Greenwich. Find the local time (a) at a place on longitude 75°E and (b) at a place on longitude 45°W.
items.solution_markdown: Time difference = longitude $\div$ 15. (a) $75 \div 15 = 5$ hours. The place is east, so it is ahead: $09{:}00 + 5\text{ h} = $ **14:00**. (b) $45 \div 15 = 3$ hours. The place is west, so it is behind: $09{:}00 - 3\text{ h} = $ **06:00**.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) A ship's captain sees the Sun at its highest point, so local time is 12:00 noon, while the chronometer set to Greenwich Mean Time reads 14:00. Find the longitude of the ship. (b) Explain why a place at 70°N has no sunset around 21 June, whereas the equator has about 12 hours of daylight on every day of the year.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Local time is 2 hours behind Greenwich, so the ship is west of Greenwich. $2 \times 15 = $ **30°W**.

(b) 70°N lies beyond the Arctic Circle (66½°N). In June the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, so such a place stays in sunlight during the whole rotation and has 24 hours of daylight. The equator is at the middle of the Earth, where the line between light and darkness always crosses the equator in two equal halves, so day and night are about equal all year.

items_markdown: Rotation (about 24 hours, west to east) causes day, night and time differences. Revolution (about 365¼ days) with the tilted axis causes the seasons.
The axis is tilted at 23½° and keeps its direction. Seasons are not caused by distance from the Sun.
Overhead Sun: about 21 March equator, 21 June Tropic of Cancer, 23 September equator, 22 December Tropic of Capricorn.
The Earth turns 15° in one hour: east is ahead, west is behind.
Proofs of the spherical shape include the disappearing ship, the curved shadow in a lunar eclipse, voyages round the world and photographs from space.
